content: The emergence of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB), including multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB) and rifampicin-resistant (RR-TB) forms, has driven the need for shorter and safer treatment regimens. In 2016, based on observational studies conducted in Asia and Africa, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended a standardized 9-month treatment regimen for eligible patients. This regimen included an injectable agent and was significantly shorter than the standard 18–20 months of care. In 2018, following the results of the STREAM Stage 1 trial, modifications were made to the shorter regimen, replacing kanamycin with amikacin due to evidence of better comparative effectiveness. However, concerns about the permanent toxic effects of injectable agents led to the development of injectable-sparing regimens. South Africa provided observational data to WHO on a 9-month all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline, which was reviewed and recommended by WHO in 2019. This regimen included a combination of bedaquiline, levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin), ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa prompted further modifications to the regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (600 mg). Additionally, the Nix-TB study by the Global TB Alliance, reviewed in 2019, evaluated a 6-month novel regimen (BPaL) consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid. This regimen showed promise in improving outcomes for patients with MDR/RR-TB and additional resistance to fluoroquinolones. However, due to limitations in study design and the small number of participants, the panel did not recommend global programmatic implementation until further evidence was available. In 2020, WHO recommended the BPaL regimen for use under operational research conditions. Two randomized controlled trials, TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, concluded in 2021, providing new evidence for WHO to assess and update recommendations for MDR/RR-TB treatment. The ZeNix trial compared different linezolid doses and durations within the BPaL regimen. The 600 mg daily dose for 9 weeks (BPaL 600–9) was compared to the 1200 mg daily dose for 26 weeks (BPaL 1200–26). While the 600–9 regimen showed fewer adverse events, the evidence was of very low certainty due to small sample sizes and imbalances in participant characteristics. The panel judged the benefits of the 600–9 regimen to be small and the undesirable effects moderate, favoring the 1200–26 regimen. The COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted TB services, reversing years of progress. In 2020, there was an 18% global decline in newly diagnosed TB cases, with numbers falling to 2012 levels. Reduced access to diagnosis and treatment led to increased TB deaths, with 1.5 million deaths in 2020, including 214,000 among HIV-positive individuals. The number of people receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB also fell by 15%, with only one in three patients in need receiving care. Despite these challenges, treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB have improved globally, reaching 59% in 2018 compared to 50% in 2012. The WHO continues to emphasize the need for shorter, safer, and more effective regimens for DR-TB to optimize outcomes, reduce adverse events, and prevent further drug resistance. The BPaL regimen, particularly with linezolid at 1200 mg for 26 weeks, remains recommended under operational research conditions for patients with MDR/RR-TB and fluoroquinolone resistance. However, concerns about adverse events related to linezolid highlight the importance of identifying the optimal dose and duration for safety and efficacy. Further research and evidence are needed to refine these regimens and expand their programmatic use.
